title: Biggest Round Table of Favorites
statement:
There are n people, numbered 0 to n − 1. Person i has exactly one favorite person, favorite[i], who is never i.

You are seating a group at one round table of any size. Every invited person will only come if one of their two neighbours at the table is their favorite. Return the largest number of people you can seat.

At a table of two, each person's two neighbours are the same person.

examples.why: 0 and 1 like each other. Seat them side by side and hang a chain off each: 2, 0, 1, 3, 4 around the table. Everyone sits next to their favorite.
0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 0 is a loop, and each of them needs the next one beside them, which fills both sides. Person 4 has nowhere to sit next to 0.
The loop 0, 1, 2 seats only 3. The mutual pairs (3, 4) and (5, 6) can share one table: 3, 4, 5, 6.

hints: Draw an arrow from each person to their favorite. Every node has exactly one outgoing arrow. What shapes can such a graph have?
Each piece is one loop with trees of chains flowing into it. A loop of length 3 or more must sit alone at the table, exactly in loop order. A loop of length 2 is different: why?

A mutual pair can take the longest chain into each partner and still has both ends open. All such pair-plus-chains fit at one table together. Answer = max(longest loop, sum over mutual pairs of 2 + longest chain into each partner).

explain.intuition:
Draw an arrow i → favorite[i]. Every person has exactly one arrow out, so each connected piece is a single loop with chains of people hanging off it, all flowing toward the loop.

A loop of 3 or more people uses both neighbours of everyone in it: each person needs the next one on one side, and is needed by the previous one on the other. Nobody else fits, so such a loop seats exactly its length, alone. A mutual pair is different: a and b satisfy each other with one side each, leaving an open side on both. You can extend each side with the longest chain flowing into that partner, giving a straight line. Lines from different pairs can be placed one after another around the same table, because their two ends need nothing. So the answer is the larger of the longest loop and the total length of all pair lines.
steps: Count incoming arrows for every person.

Peel the chains like a topological sort: start a queue with everyone nobody likes. When you pop u, set depth[favorite[u]] = max(depth[favorite[u]], depth[u] + 1) and decrease its in-degree; push it when that reaches 0.
Whoever is left is on a loop. Walk each loop once to get its length.
For a loop of length 2 with members a and b, add 2 + depth[a] + depth[b] to pairTotal. For longer loops, update bestLoop.
pitfalls: Taking only the single best mutual pair. Several pair lines share one table, so they add up.
Hanging chains on a loop of length 3 or more. Its members have no free side.
Adding both of two chains that flow into the same partner. Only one chain fits on that partner's open side, so take the longest.

solutions.title: Try every seating order
solutions.idea: Build every sequence of distinct people, treat it as a circle, and keep the longest one where everyone sits next to their favorite.

solutions.title: Peel chains, then measure loops
solutions.idea: A topological peel gives the longest chain into every node and leaves only loop members. Long loops sit alone; mutual pairs with their chains add up.

followups: Return one valid seating order for the best answer, not just its size.
People may list two favorites and be happy if either is a neighbour. Does the loop-and-chain structure still hold?
